title: When Leaders Must Choose the Least Worst Option
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Drawing on the wrenching dilemma in William Styron's Sophie's Choice, this Field Note addresses decisions where every available option is genuinely bad. The first step is accepting there's no way to reframe the situation into a positive outcome -- a hard adjustment for optimistic leaders. From there, decision-makers should apply their values and weigh long-term versus short-term consequences to build a rough hierarchy of pain, since predicting unintended consequences is never fully possible. The piece closes by arguing that how leaders handle these worst-case decisions, not the easy ones, is what actually reveals their character.
points: Some decisions offer only bad options, requiring leaders to select the least worst rather than a positive outcome.
Accepting that no reframing will produce a positive choice is presented as a necessary first step.
Values and long-term versus short-term thinking help build a rough hierarchy of which bad option causes least harm.
Unintended consequences of each option can never be fully known but must be estimated as carefully as possible.
The piece argues that hardest, least-worst decisions -- not easy ones -- reveal a leader's true character.
quotes: Decisions, like the one Styron poses, are more complex than no-win or lose-lose situations.
Accepting that the options available are all negative and there is no way to reframe or recast the situation to create a positive choice and outcome is a critical first step.
Applying values, preferred consequences, and long-term versus short-term thinking helps decision-makers to create a hierarchy of pain.

The goal of choosing the least worst option offers a frame from which to act rather than to become paralyzed by the distaste of having to select from a set of choices that are highly flawed or plagued by negative ramifications.
Great leaders are never defined by the easy decisions they make. It is with the hardest of calls that reveals to the world who leaders really are.
